[2020 summer phd math-stat — problem 1]

Suppose $(Y_1, \dots, Y_n)$ are observed, where $Y_i = \max(0, X_i)$ and $(X_1, \dots, X_n)$ are i.i.d. $N(\mu^*, \sigma^{*2})$ with $(\mu^*, \sigma^*)$ unknown. Define $R_i = \mathbb{1}\{Y_i > 0\}$. Let $\Phi(\cdot)$ be the $N(0,1)$ CDF. For $\theta = (\beta, \sigma)$ with $\beta = \mu/\sigma$, let $P_\theta$ denote $N(\mu, \sigma^2)$, and $\theta^* = (\beta^*, \sigma^*)$.
(i) Define an estimator $\hat\theta_1 = (\hat\beta_1, \hat\sigma_1)$ as the solution of $\mathbb{E}_\theta(R_1) = \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n R_i$ and $\mathbb{E}_\theta(R_1 Y_1) = \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n R_i Y_i$. Find closed-form expressions for $(\hat\beta_1, \hat\sigma_1)$ (you may use $\Phi$ and its inverse).
(ii) Show that $(\hat\beta_1, \hat\sigma_1)$ are consistent estimators of $(\beta^*, \sigma^*)$.
(iii) Show that $\sqrt{n}(\hat\theta_1 - \theta^*) \xrightarrow{D} N(0, \tau_1)$ for some variance $\tau_1$; find a closed-form expression for $\tau_1$.
(iv) Write down the log-likelihood $\ell(\theta)$, and compute $\mathbb{E}_\theta\{\frac1n \frac{\partial \ell(\theta)}{\partial \theta}\}$ and $n\operatorname{var}_\theta\{\frac1n \frac{\partial \ell(\theta)}{\partial \theta}\}$ in closed form.
(v) The MLE $\hat\theta_2 = (\hat\beta_2, \hat\sigma_2)$ satisfies $\sqrt{n}(\hat\theta_2 - \theta^*) \xrightarrow{D} N(0, \tau_2)$ (you need not prove this). Find a closed-form expression for $\tau_2$.
(vi) Show that $\tau_1 \ge \tau_2$. Give a direct proof, instead of invoking the asymptotic efficiency of maximum likelihood estimation.

Let \(\varphi=\Phi'\) denote the standard normal density. For a generic \(\theta=(\beta,\sigma)\), write

\[
p=\Phi(\beta),\qquad q=\Phi(-\beta)=1-p,\qquad a=\varphi(\beta),
\]
\[
m=m(\beta):=\beta \Phi(\beta)+\varphi(\beta)=\beta p+a.
\]

Also write \(X=\sigma(\beta+Z)\) with \(Z\sim N(0,1)\).

---

## (i) Closed-form \((\hat\beta_1,\hat\sigma_1)\)

Since \(R=\mathbf 1\{Y>0\}=\mathbf 1\{X>0\}\),

\[
\mathbb E_\theta R=P_\theta(X>0)=P(Z>-\beta)=\Phi(\beta)=p.
\]

Also,

\[
\mathbb E_\theta(RY)=\mathbb E_\theta[X\mathbf 1\{X>0\}]
=\sigma \mathbb E\{(\beta+Z)\mathbf 1(Z>-\beta)\}.
\]

Using

\[
\mathbb E[Z\mathbf 1(Z>-\beta)]=\varphi(\beta)=a,
\]

we get

\[
\mathbb E_\theta(RY)=\sigma\{\beta\Phi(\beta)+\varphi(\beta)\}
=\sigma m(\beta).
\]

Let

\[
\bar R=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n R_i,\qquad 
\overline{RY}=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n R_iY_i.
\]

The moment equations are

\[
\Phi(\hat\beta_1)=\bar R,
\qquad 
\hat\sigma_1 m(\hat\beta_1)=\overline{RY}.
\]

Thus, on the event \(0<\bar R<1\),

\[
\boxed{\hat\beta_1=\Phi^{-1}(\bar R)}
\]

and

\[
\boxed{
\hat\sigma_1
=
\frac{\overline{RY}}
{\hat\beta_1\Phi(\hat\beta_1)+\varphi(\hat\beta_1)}
=
\frac{\overline{RY}}
{\hat\beta_1\bar R+\varphi(\hat\beta_1)}
}.
\]

If \(\bar R\in\{0,1\}\), no finite solution exists; however, under the true model \(P(\bar R\in\{0,1\})\to0\), so this does not affect asymptotics. One may define the estimator arbitrarily on that negligible event.

---

## (ii) Consistency

At the true parameter \(\theta^*=(\beta^*,\sigma^*)\),

\[
\mathbb E_{\theta^*}R=\Phi(\beta^*)=:p^*
\]

and

\[
\mathbb E_{\theta^*}(RY)=\sigma^* m(\beta^*).
\]

By the strong law of large numbers,

\[
\bar R\xrightarrow{a.s.} p^*
\]

and

\[
\overline{RY}\xrightarrow{a.s.}\sigma^*m(\beta^*).
\]

Since \(\Phi^{-1}\) is continuous on \((0,1)\),

\[
\hat\beta_1=\Phi^{-1}(\bar R)\xrightarrow{a.s.}\Phi^{-1}(p^*)=\beta^*.
\]

Also \(m(\beta)=\beta\Phi(\beta)+\varphi(\beta)>0\) for every finite \(\beta\), and \(m\) is continuous. Hence

\[
m(\hat\beta_1)\xrightarrow{a.s.}m(\beta^*),
\]

so

\[
\hat\sigma_1
=
\frac{\overline{RY}}{m(\hat\beta_1)}
\xrightarrow{a.s.}
\frac{\sigma^*m(\beta^*)}{m(\beta^*)}
=\sigma^*.
\]

Therefore,

\[
\boxed{\hat\theta_1=(\hat\beta_1,\hat\sigma_1)\xrightarrow{P}\theta^*.}
\]

---

## (iii) Asymptotic distribution of \(\hat\theta_1\)

Let

\[
W_i=
\begin{pmatrix}
R_i\\
R_iY_i
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad 
\gamma(\theta)=\mathbb E_\theta W_i
=
\begin{pmatrix}
p\\
\sigma m
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

We need \(\operatorname{Var}_\theta(W_i)\). First,

\[
\operatorname{Var}(R)=p(1-p)=pq.
\]

Next,

\[
\operatorname{Cov}(R,RY)
=
\mathbb E(RY)-\mathbb E R\,\mathbb E(RY)
=
\sigma m-\sigma pm
=
\sigma mq.
\]

Finally,

\[
\mathbb E(RY)^2
=
\mathbb E[X^2\mathbf 1\{X>0\}]
=
\sigma^2\mathbb E[(\beta+Z)^2\mathbf 1(Z>-\beta)].
\]

Using

\[
\mathbb E[Z^2\mathbf 1(Z>-\beta)]
=
\Phi(\beta)-\beta\varphi(\beta)
=
p-\beta a,
\]

we get

\[
\mathbb E[(\beta+Z)^2\mathbf 1(Z>-\beta)]
=
(\beta^2+1)p+\beta a.
\]

Define

\[
v=v(\beta):=(\beta^2+1)p+\beta a.
\]

Then

\[
\operatorname{Var}(RY)=\sigma^2(v-m^2).
\]

Thus

\[
\Sigma_W(\theta):=\operatorname{Var}_\theta(W_i)
=
\begin{pmatrix}
pq & \sigma mq\\
\sigma mq & \sigma^2(v-m^2)
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

The Jacobian of \(\gamma\) is

\[
G(\theta)
=
\frac{\partial \gamma(\theta)}{\partial \theta^\top}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
a & 0\\
\sigma p & m
\end{pmatrix},
\]

because \(m'(\beta)=\Phi(\beta)=p\). Hence

\[
G(\theta)^{-1}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
a^{-1} & 0\\[4pt]
-\dfrac{\sigma p}{am} & m^{-1}
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

By the multivariate CLT and the delta method,

\[
\sqrt n(\hat\theta_1-\theta^*)
\overset{D}{\longrightarrow}
N(0,\tau_1),
\]

where

\[
\boxed{
\tau_1
=
G(\theta^*)^{-1}\Sigma_W(\theta^*)G(\theta^*)^{-T}.
}
\]

Equivalently, writing \(p,q,a,m,v,\sigma\) evaluated at \(\theta^*\),

\[
\boxed{
\tau_1
=
\begin{pmatrix}
\dfrac{pq}{a^2}
&
\dfrac{\sigma q}{a}\left(1-\dfrac{p^2}{am}\right)
\\[12pt]
\dfrac{\sigma q}{a}\left(1-\dfrac{p^2}{am}\right)
&
\dfrac{\sigma^2}{m^2}
\left[
v-m^2-\dfrac{2pqm}{a}+\dfrac{p^3q}{a^2}
\right]
\end{pmatrix}.
}
\]

---

## (iv) Log-likelihood and score moments

The observed distribution has an atom at \(0\) of mass \(q=\Phi(-\beta)\), and for \(y>0\) has density

\[
f_\theta(y)=\frac1\sigma \varphi\left(\frac y\sigma-\beta\right).
\]

Therefore the log-likelihood is

\[
\ell(\theta)
=
\sum_{i=1}^n
\left[
(1-R_i)\log \Phi(-\beta)
+
R_i\left\{
-\log\sigma+\log\varphi\left(\frac{Y_i}{\sigma}-\beta\right)
\right\}
\right].
\]

Equivalently,

\[
\ell(\theta)
=
\sum_{i=1}^n
\left[
(1-R_i)\log q
+
R_i\left\{
-\log\sigma-\frac12\left(\frac{Y_i}{\sigma}-\beta\right)^2-\frac12\log(2\pi)
\right\}
\right].
\]

Let

\[
Z_i(\theta)=\frac{Y_i}{\sigma}-\beta.
\]

The one-observation score components are

\[
S_{\beta,i}
=
R_i Z_i(\theta)
-
(1-R_i)\frac{a}{q},
\]

and

\[
S_{\sigma,i}
=
\frac{R_i}{\sigma}
\left[
Z_i(\theta)\frac{Y_i}{\sigma}-1
\right]
=
\frac{R_i}{\sigma}
\left[
Z_i(\theta)^2+\beta Z_i(\theta)-1
\right].
\]

Hence

\[
\frac{\partial \ell(\theta)}{\partial \theta}
=
\sum_{i=1}^n
\begin{pmatrix}
S_{\beta,i}\\
S_{\sigma,i}
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

Under \(P_\theta\), the score has mean zero:

\[
\boxed{
\mathbb E_\theta\left\{\frac1n\frac{\partial\ell(\theta)}{\partial\theta}\right\}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
0\\
0
\end{pmatrix}.
}
\]

Now compute the covariance. Since observations are independent,

\[
n\operatorname{Var}_\theta\left\{\frac1n\frac{\partial\ell(\theta)}{\partial\theta}\right\}
=
\operatorname{Var}_\theta(S_{\theta,1})
=
\mathcal I(\theta),
\]

the Fisher information for one observation.

Using truncated normal identities,

\[
\int_{-\beta}^\infty z\varphi(z)\,dz=a,
\]

\[
\int_{-\beta}^\infty z^2\varphi(z)\,dz=p-\beta a,
\]

\[
\int_{-\beta}^\infty z^3\varphi(z)\,dz=(\beta^2+2)a,
\]

and

\[
\int_{-\beta}^\infty z^4\varphi(z)\,dz=3p-(\beta^3+3\beta)a,
\]

one obtains

\[
\mathcal I(\theta)
=
\begin{pmatrix}
A & B/\sigma\\[4pt]
B/\sigma & C/\sigma^2
\end{pmatrix},
\]

where

\[
A=p-\beta a+\frac{a^2}{q},
\]

\[
B=\beta p+a=m,
\]

and

\[
C=(\beta^2+2)p+\beta a.
\]

Thus

\[
\boxed{
n\operatorname{Var}_\theta\left\{\frac1n\frac{\partial\ell(\theta)}{\partial\theta}\right\}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
p-\beta a+\dfrac{a^2}{q}
&
\dfrac{\beta p+a}{\sigma}
\\[12pt]
\dfrac{\beta p+a}{\sigma}
&
\dfrac{(\beta^2+2)p+\beta a}{\sigma^2}
\end{pmatrix}.
}
\]

---

## (v) Asymptotic variance \(\tau_2\) of the MLE

By the standard asymptotic normality of the MLE,

\[
\sqrt n(\hat\theta_2-\theta^*)
\overset{D}{\longrightarrow}
N(0,\tau_2),
\]

with

\[
\tau_2=\mathcal I(\theta^*)^{-1}.
\]

Using the notation from part (iv), evaluated at \(\theta^*\), define

\[
\Delta=AC-B^2.
\]

Then

\[
\mathcal I(\theta^*)^{-1}
=
\frac1{\Delta}
\begin{pmatrix}
C & -\sigma B\\
-\sigma B & \sigma^2 A
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

Therefore

\[
\boxed{
\tau_2
=
\frac1{AC-B^2}
\begin{pmatrix}
C & -\sigma B\\
-\sigma B & \sigma^2 A
\end{pmatrix}_{\theta=\theta^*},
}
\]

where

\[
A=p-\beta a+\frac{a^2}{q},\qquad 
B=\beta p+a,\qquad 
C=(\beta^2+2)p+\beta a.
\]

---

## (vi) Direct proof that \(\tau_1\ge \tau_2\)

We prove the Loewner-order inequality

\[
\boxed{\tau_1-\tau_2 \text{ is positive semidefinite}.}
\]

Let

\[
W=
\begin{pmatrix}
R\\
RY
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad 
\gamma(\theta)=\mathbb E_\theta W,
\]

and let \(S_\theta\) be the one-observation score vector. From part (iii),

\[
\tau_1=\operatorname{Var}_{\theta^*}(\psi),
\]

where the influence function of \(\hat\theta_1\) is

\[
\psi
=
G(\theta^*)^{-1}\{W-\gamma(\theta^*)\}.
\]

Also, from part (iv),

\[
\tau_2=\mathcal I(\theta^*)^{-1},
\qquad 
\mathcal I(\theta^*)=\operatorname{Var}_{\theta^*}(S_{\theta^*}).
\]

Now use the score identity. Since

\[
G(\theta)
=
\frac{\partial \gamma(\theta)}{\partial \theta^\top},
\]

we have

\[
G(\theta)
=
\mathbb E_\theta\left[\{W-\gamma(\theta)\}S_\theta^\top\right].
\]

Therefore, at \(\theta^*\),

\[
\mathbb E_{\theta^*}[\psi S_{\theta^*}^\top]
=
G(\theta^*)^{-1}
\mathbb E_{\theta^*}\left[\{W-\gamma(\theta^*)\}S_{\theta^*}^\top\right]
=
G(\theta^*)^{-1}G(\theta^*)
=
I_2.
\]

Hence

\[
\begin{aligned}
\tau_1-\tau_2
&=
\operatorname{Var}(\psi)-\mathcal I^{-1} \\
&=
\mathbb E\left[
\{\psi-\mathcal I^{-1}S\}
\{\psi-\mathcal I^{-1}S\}^\top
\right],
\end{aligned}
\]

where all expectations and \(\mathcal I\) are evaluated at \(\theta^*\).

Indeed, expanding the right-hand side gives

\[
\operatorname{Var}(\psi)
-
\mathbb E[\psi S^\top]\mathcal I^{-1}
-
\mathcal I^{-1}\mathbb E[S\psi^\top]
+
\mathcal I^{-1}\mathbb E[SS^\top]\mathcal I^{-1}
=
\tau_1-\mathcal I^{-1}.
\]

Since

\[
\mathbb E[\psi S^\top]=I_2,
\qquad 
\mathbb E[SS^\top]=\mathcal I,
\]

this equals \(\tau_1-\tau_2\).

The matrix

\[
\mathbb E\left[
\{\psi-\mathcal I^{-1}S\}
\{\psi-\mathcal I^{-1}S\}^\top
\right]
\]

is positive semidefinite. Therefore,

\[
\boxed{\tau_1\ge \tau_2.}
\]

This proof is direct and does not invoke the general asymptotic efficiency theorem for maximum likelihood estimators.

\tau_1
=
G(\theta^*)^{-1}\Sigma_W(\theta^*)G(\theta^*)^{-T}.
}
\]

Equivalently, writing \(p,q,a,m,v,\sigma\) evaluated at \(\theta^*\),

\[
\boxed{
\tau_1
=
\begin{pmatrix}
\dfrac{pq}{a^2}
&
\dfrac{\sigma q}{a}\left(1-\dfrac{p^2}{am}\right)
\\[12pt]
\dfrac{\sigma q}{a}\left(1-\dfrac{p^2}{am}\right)
&
\dfrac{\sigma^2}{m^2}
\left[
v-m^2-\dfrac{2pqm}{a}+\dfrac{p^3q}{a^2}
\right]
\end{pmatrix}.
}
\]

---

## (iv) Log-likelihood and score moments

The observed distribution has an atom at \(0\) of mass \(q=\Phi(-\beta)\), and for \(y>0\) has density

\[
f_\theta(y)=\frac1\sigma \varphi\left(\frac y\sigma-\beta\right).
\]

Therefore the log-likelihood is

\[
\ell(\theta)
=
\sum_{i=1}^n
\left[
(1-R_i)\log \Phi(-\beta)
+
R_i\left\{
-\log\sigma+\log\varphi\left(\frac{Y_i}{\sigma}-\beta\right)
\right\}
\right].
\]

Equivalently,

\[
\ell(\theta)
=
\sum_{i=1}^n
\left[
(1-R_i)\log q
+
R_i\left\{
-\log\sigma-\frac12\left(\frac{Y_i}{\sigma}-\beta\right)^2-\frac12\log(2\pi)
\right\}
\right].
\]

Let

\[
Z_i(\theta)=\frac{Y_i}{\sigma}-\beta.
\]

The one-observation score components are

\[
S_{\beta,i}
=
R_i Z_i(\theta)
-
(1-R_i)\frac{a}{q},
\]

and

\[
S_{\sigma,i}
=
\frac{R_i}{\sigma}
\left[
Z_i(\theta)\frac{Y_i}{\sigma}-1
\right]
=
\frac{R_i}{\sigma}
\left[
Z_i(\theta)^2+\beta Z_i(\theta)-1
\right].
\]

Hence

\[
\frac{\partial \ell(\theta)}{\partial \theta}
=
\sum_{i=1}^n
\begin{pmatrix}
S_{\beta,i}\\
S_{\sigma,i}
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

Under \(P_\theta\), the score has mean zero:

\[
\boxed{
\mathbb E_\theta\left\{\frac1n\frac{\partial\ell(\theta)}{\partial\theta}\right\}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
0\\
0
\end{pmatrix}.
}
\]

Now compute the covariance. Since observations are independent,

\[
n\operatorname{Var}_\theta\left\{\frac1n\frac{\partial\ell(\theta)}{\partial\theta}\right\}
=
\operatorname{Var}_\theta(S_{\theta,1})
=
\mathcal I(\theta),
\]

the Fisher information for one observation.

Using truncated normal identities,

\[
\int_{-\beta}^\infty z\varphi(z)\,dz=a,
\]

\[
\int_{-\beta}^\infty z^2\varphi(z)\,dz=p-\beta a,
\]

\[
\int_{-\beta}^\infty z^3\varphi(z)\,dz=(\beta^2+2)a,
\]

and

\[
\int_{-\beta}^\infty z^4\varphi(z)\,dz=3p-(\beta^3+3\beta)a,
\]

one obtains

\[
\mathcal I(\theta)
=
\begin{pmatrix}
A & B/\sigma\\[4pt]
B/\sigma & C/\sigma^2
\end{pmatrix},
\]

where

\[
A=p-\beta a+\frac{a^2}{q},
\]

\[
B=\beta p+a=m,
\]

and

\[
C=(\beta^2+2)p+\beta a.
\]

Thus

\[
\boxed{
n\operatorname{Var}_\theta\left\{\frac1n\frac{\partial\ell(\theta)}{\partial\theta}\right\}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
p-\beta a+\dfrac{a^2}{q}
&
\dfrac{\beta p+a}{\sigma}
\\[12pt]
\dfrac{\beta p+a}{\sigma}
&
\dfrac{(\beta^2+2)p+\beta a}{\sigma^2}
\end{pmatrix}.
}
\]

---

## (v) Asymptotic variance \(\tau_2\) of the MLE

By the standard asymptotic normality of the MLE,

\[
\sqrt n(\hat\theta_2-\theta^*)
\overset{D}{\longrightarrow}
N(0,\tau_2),
\]

with

\[
\tau_2=\mathcal I(\theta^*)^{-1}.
\]

Using the notation from part (iv), evaluated at \(\theta^*\), define

\[
\Delta=AC-B^2.
\]

Then

\[
\mathcal I(\theta^*)^{-1}
=
\frac1{\Delta}
\begin{pmatrix}
C & -\sigma B\\
-\sigma B & \sigma^2 A
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

Therefore

\[
\boxed{
\tau_2
=
\frac1{AC-B^2}
\begin{pmatrix}
C & -\sigma B\\
-\sigma B & \sigma^2 A
\end{pmatrix}_{\theta=\theta^*},
}
\]

where

\[
A=p-\beta a+\frac{a^2}{q},\qquad 
B=\beta p+a,\qquad 
C=(\beta^2+2)p+\beta a.
\]

---

## (vi) Direct proof that \(\tau_1\ge \tau_2\)

We prove the Loewner-order inequality

\[
\boxed{\tau_1-\tau_2 \text{ is positive semidefinite}.}
\]

Let

\[
W=
\begin{pmatrix}
R\\
RY
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad 
\gamma(\theta)=\mathbb E_\theta W,
\]

and let \(S_\theta\) be the one-observation score vector. From part (iii),

\[
\tau_1=\operatorname{Var}_{\theta^*}(\psi),
\]

where the influence function of \(\hat\theta_1\) is

\[
\psi
=
G(\theta^*)^{-1}\{W-\gamma(\theta^*)\}.
\]

Also, from part (iv),

\[
\tau_2=\mathcal I(\theta^*)^{-1},
\qquad 
\mathcal I(\theta^*)=\operatorname{Var}_{\theta^*}(S_{\theta^*}).
\]

Now use the score identity. Since

\[
G(\theta)
=
\frac{\partial \gamma(\theta)}{\partial \theta^\top},
\]

we have

\[
G(\theta)
=
\mathbb E_\theta\left[\{W-\gamma(\theta)\}S_\theta^\top\right].
\]

Therefore, at \(\theta^*\),

\[
\mathbb E_{\theta^*}[\psi S_{\theta^*}^\top]
=
G(\theta^*)^{-1}
\mathbb E_{\theta^*}\left[\{W-\gamma(\theta^*)\}S_{\theta^*}^\top\right]
=
G(\theta^*)^{-1}G(\theta^*)
=
I_2.
\]

Hence

\[
\begin{aligned}
\tau_1-\tau_2
&=
\operatorname{Var}(\psi)-\mathcal I^{-1} \\
&=
\mathbb E\left[
\{\psi-\mathcal I^{-1}S\}
\{\psi-\mathcal I^{-1}S\}^\top
\right],
\end{aligned}
\]

where all expectations and \(\mathcal I\) are evaluated at \(\theta^*\).

Indeed, expanding the right-hand side gives

\[
\operatorname{Var}(\psi)
-
\mathbb E[\psi S^\top]\mathcal I^{-1}
-
\mathcal I^{-1}\mathbb E[S\psi^\top]
+
\mathcal I^{-1}\mathbb E[SS^\top]\mathcal I^{-1}
=
\tau_1-\mathcal I^{-1}.
\]

Since

\[
\mathbb E[\psi S^\top]=I_2,
\qquad 
\mathbb E[SS^\top]=\mathcal I,
\]

this equals \(\tau_1-\tau_2\).

The matrix

\[
\mathbb E\left[
\{\psi-\mathcal I^{-1}S\}
\{\psi-\mathcal I^{-1}S\}^\top
\right]
\]

is positive semidefinite. Therefore,

\[
\boxed{\tau_1\ge \tau_2.}
\]

This proof is direct and does not invoke the general asymptotic efficiency theorem for maximum likelihood estimators.
